source.title: Uncertainty Based Detection and Relabeling of Noisy Image Labels
source.authors: J. Köhler; Maximilian Autenrieth; William H. Beluch

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures learning over training on symmetrically corrupted labels and reports that the network can predict true labels for noisy examples before overfitting to their labels. This bears on V6, but it does not reproduce the original random-label experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper mentions fitting randomly assigned labels only as a result from cited work [33]; that is not a row. Other results concern the authors’ uncertainty-based detection and relabeling method, rather than the claim versions.
record.test_reason: Figure 3a reports the network's own learning dynamics under 40% symmetric label noise: it predicts true labels early and later fits corrupted labels. These results directly test V6, although the paper's main purpose is noise detection and relabeling.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that ensemble plus MC-dropout uncertainty identifies noisy labels and that early predictions can guide relabeling. Their predicted-label procedure nearly halves label noise without improving classification accuracy; oracle relabeling improves accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses symmetric and pair label corruption with uncertainty-based detection and relabeling; it does not run the original random-label fitting experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported relabeling point depends on training epoch; the paper describes different uncertainty heuristics for identifying that point.
record.problems: The result relevant to V6 is for one stated dataset and one stated symmetric noise level. The paper reports no uncertainty estimate for the 80% figure and does not include a separate random-label comparison.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results directly measure a behavior named by the claim versions. The uncertainty detection and iterative relabeling outcomes in Sections 3–4 and Tables 1–2 concern the proposed method, not those versions.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters are not tested.
Relative training time and convergence speed across corruption fractions are not measured.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs is not tested.
Perfect training fit and steadily degrading test performance across corruption fractions from none to all are not tested. Iterative relabeling changes which examples remain noisy.
The necessity or sufficiency of explicit regularization is not tested.
Fully random labels, separate real-label versus random-label training conditions, and generality across architectures and noise levels are not tested by the reported learning-order result.

missing.what: Late-training memorization: the authors explicitly state that the network ultimately predicts the noisy labels perfectly. Record this endpoint alongside early true-label prediction to capture the full temporal comparison.
missing.locator: Section 3, Relabeling of noisy labels, Figure 3a and accompanying text

record.verdict_notes: The random-label fitting statement in the introduction is attributed to prior work and supplies no independent evidence for V1. The 80% result measures recovery of true labels on corrupted examples, not accuracy against their assigned noisy labels.

versions.untested_parts: The paper cites this result from [33] but does not test random-label fitting, chance test error, or unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training time and convergence as the fraction of corrupted labels changes are not tested.
Shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, and Gaussian-noise inputs are not tested.
The paper does not measure perfect training fit and test error across corruption fractions from none to all.
The necessity or sufficiency of weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation for fitting random labels or generalizing on true labels is not tested.
The paper studies 40% symmetric label noise, not fully random labels; it does not compare learning dynamics on real labels against a separate random-label condition.

rows.subject: simple convolutional network described in [3]
rows.operation_detail: Measured classification accuracy over training on CIFAR-10 with 40% symmetric label noise, including accuracy on noisy images against their true labels.
rows.measure: Classification accuracy of clean and noisy training images over epochs; the text reports that by around epoch 15 the network could correctly relabel 80% of noisy images.
rows.value: Around epoch 15, the network had learned enough from clean images to correctly relabel 80% of noisy images, before overfitting to noisy labels began.
rows.note: The 80% figure is stated in the text; the accompanying plot shows accuracy over training. The paper does not provide a separate random-label condition.
rows.check: The early 80% true-label accuracy is correctly extracted. Include the accompanying late-training result: the network eventually predicts the noisy labels perfectly. Together these establish the learning order described by V6.

relationships.reason: R1 reports 80% true-label accuracy on noisy examples around epoch 15 before overfitting; the accompanying text explicitly reports eventual perfect prediction of noisy labels.
relationships.display_finding: True-label accuracy on noisy examples reached 80% around epoch 15 before overfitting, with eventual perfect prediction of the supplied noisy labels.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
